summary: This Standards Track document defines SCIM security events using Security Event Tokens (RFC 8417), so SCIM service providers and receivers can exchange messages asynchronously. It updates RFC 7643 with extra ServiceProviderConfig attributes and RFC 7644 with an optional new capability.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of repeatedly asking whether the list changed, the system sends a short note whenever something happens.

questions: what is a scim security event
how do asynchronous scim requests work
subtitle: SCIM events carried in Security Event Tokens, so identity systems can push change notices and finish async requests.

tldr.problem: When several SCIM clients change resources, other parties fall out of date. Polling with repeated GET requests becomes costly as changes and resources grow, and long requests tie up HTTP connections.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines SCIM event URIs carried in Security Event Tokens (RFC 8417): feed, provisioning and asynchronous-completion events. It adds the Prefer: respond-async request, a Set-Txn response header, and a securityEvents discovery attribute.
tldr.outcome: Receivers learn only about changes and decide their own follow-up. The RFC updates RFC 7643 and RFC 7644 and creates an IANA registry of SCIM event URIs.

today: RFC 9967 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2026. It updates RFC 7643 with new ServiceProviderConfig attributes and RFC 7644 with an optional asynchronous request capability, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why SCIM Needs Events
sections.content:
SCIM clients change resources with HTTP methods such as POST, PATCH and DELETE. When many independent clients do this, each one goes out of date. Polling with periodic GET requests becomes a problem as the number of changes and resources increases.

RFC 9967 instead shares Security Events using Security Event Tokens (SETs, RFC 8417) over an event feed. A SET describes a state change at a SCIM service provider. It is not a command: each Event Receiver decides its own best follow-up action, such as reconciling schema or resource-type differences between domains.

The document defines three kinds of event (resource feed changes, provisioning changes and asynchronous request completion) and uses the HTTP header Prefer: respond-async (RFC 7240) so a client can ask for an asynchronous response.
sections.plainLanguage: A SET is a short note saying what changed. The person who gets the note decides what to do about it.

sections.title: Subjects and Common Attributes
sections.content:
A SCIM event is a SET whose events claim holds one or more event URIs beginning with urn:ietf:params:scim:event. Events fall into the feed and prov sub-namespaces, and a misc class covers asynchronous completion.

Events MUST identify their subject with the sub_id claim (RFC 9493) in the main JWT claims, not inside an event payload. The JWT sub claim MUST NOT be used, to avoid confusion with authorization tokens. Its format is scim, and it carries a required uri (the relative path, such as a /Users/... path), plus an optional externalId and id. Other attributes whose uniqueness is server or global may be added when those are not enough.

Common attributes are txn (identifies a transaction at the service provider and stays the same across retransmission or multiple receivers, unlike the per-token jti), version (the resource ETag), and either data or attributes, never both.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note says whose record changed, using the name on the file folder. A transaction number lets you match several copies of the same news.

sections.title: Feed, Provisioning and Misc Events
sections.content:
Feed events (feed:add, feed:remove) say a resource joined or left an event feed. Adding does not mean the resource is new, and removing does not mean it was deleted.

Provisioning events cover create, patch and put, each in a full form (the data attribute holds the final representation) or a notice form (the attributes attribute lists what changed). delete has no payload and no full/notice qualifier, and no feed:remove is issued alongside it. activate and deactivate signal that an account is ready for use or disabled, with the exact meaning agreed between publisher and receiver.

The misc:asyncresp event signals completion of an asynchronous request.
sections.plainLanguage: Some notes say everything that changed; others just say that something changed so you can go look. Delete notes are simply "this one is gone".

sections.title: Asynchronous Requests and Set-Txn
sections.content:
A client can add Prefer: respond-async to a POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE. The wait preference SHOULD be supported to set a maximum time before the provider may answer asynchronously. The provider returns either a normal SCIM response or HTTP status 202 (Accepted) with no body. A 202 response MUST carry the new Set-Txn header, whose value MUST match the txn claim of the later completion SET. It also includes Preference-Applied and a Location header.

For a SCIM bulk request with asynchronous handling, one completion event MUST be generated per operation. Each txn is the original value, a colon, and the zero-based operation index, for example 2d80e537a3f64622b0347b641ebc8f44:0. The bulkId MUST NOT be used for this. If processing fails, the event includes a response attribute with the SCIM error details.

Intermediaries SHOULD NOT insert, modify or delete the Set-Txn value, and clients MAY ignore it when confirmation is not needed.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand in a big job and get a claim ticket right away. Later a note arrives with the same ticket number telling you whether the job worked.

sections.title: Discovering Event Support
sections.content:
RFC 9967 adds an optional complex attribute, securityEvents, to the ServiceProviderConfig schema. When it is absent, the provider does not support or is not configured for Security Events.

Its sub-attribute asyncRequest is a case-insensitive string: none (no asynchronous requests), long (the server completes asynchronously at its own discretion, for instance after a maximum wait) or request (asynchronously when the client asks). The sub-attribute eventUris lists the event URIs the server can deliver through a SET stream. It is informational only; stream registration and configuration are out of scope.

IANA created a "SCIM Event URIs" registry with Expert Review and registered the Set-Txn header field name.
sections.plainLanguage: A sign on the door says whether this office sends notes, and which kinds.

sections.title: Two Ways to Use the Events
sections.content:
The appendix describes two non-normative modes. In Domain-Based Replication (DBR), replicas in one administrative domain stay in sync, and events usually use the full variant, so no callback is needed.

In Coordinated Provisioning (CP), events act as change notices without raw data, and the receiver calls back (for example with a SCIM GET) to fetch the new state. The RFC lists benefits: differing schemas, per-receiver access rights and data filtering, independent decisions about what to accept, and the ability to throttle or buffer. The cost is a possible callback per event, though a receiver need not call back on every event.
sections.plainLanguage: In one mode, everyone gets a full copy of the news. In the other, you get a short heads-up and ask for details only if you want them.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The security and privacy sections of RFC 8417, RFC 8935 and RFC 8936 also apply. SETs may contain personally identifiable information, so transmitters and recipients MUST protect them in transit with TLS. Receivers MUST persist events directly or indirectly before acknowledging them. Access to event recovery and forwarding MUST be limited to the parties that need it.

When the publisher does not talk directly to the receiver, receivers MUST verify the originator using JWS signatures (RFC 7515). The URI returned for an asynchronous result MUST be protected and require an Authorization header or other client authentication.

For busy resources such as large Groups, the RFC recommends SCIM PATCH instead of PUT, or using the notice events with periodic GETs, or aggregating several PATCH changes into one event.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes can contain private details, so they travel in sealed envelopes and only the right people may open the mailbox.
